title: What Can India's New 25-Qubit Quantum Computer Actually Do?
meta_title: What Can India's New 25-Qubit Quantum Computer Actually Do? | Aperture
summary: MIT Bengaluru opened India's first quantum hub with a 25-qubit system in October 2026. Here's what that actually means, and what it doesn't.
primary_question: What can India's new 25-qubit quantum computer actually do?
key_takeaways: MIT Bengaluru's Quantum-Hub@MAHE opened October 13, 2026 with a 25-qubit open-architecture system

content:
A 25-qubit quantum computer is a research and training tool. At that scale, it can run basic quantum algorithms, test error-correction approaches, and give engineers hands-on experience with quantum hardware. It cannot break encryption, simulate complex drug molecules, or outperform your laptop on any real task. India now has one, and that matters, but probably not for the reasons the press releases suggest.

Key Takeaways

  • MIT Bengaluru's Quantum-Hub@MAHE opened October 13, 2026 with a 25-qubit open-architecture system
  • 25 qubits is a research-grade facility, far from commercial use; IBM operates above 1,000 qubits
  • The real win is workforce: the hub targets 100 trained quantum engineers by December 2026
  • India's National Quantum Mission aims for 1,000-qubit indigenous systems by 2028 to 2031
  • Practical quantum advantage for industry is realistically 10 or more years out

What Actually Opened at MIT Bengaluru?

Quantum-Hub@MAHE, operated by Manipal Institute of Technology in Bengaluru, inaugurated on October 13, 2026. The core hardware is a 25-qubit open-architecture dilution refrigeration system, meaning the qubits are cooled to near absolute zero to maintain their quantum state. Partners include QuantrolOx (a spin-out from the University of Oxford), Bluefors (a Finnish cryogenic hardware maker), Qblox, and ConScience. The goal is to train 100 quantum engineers by December 2026, support start-up incubation, and serve as a testbed for indigenous hardware development. Longer-term, the roadmap targets a 150-qubit system and eventually industrial systems above 1,000 qubits.

What Does 25 Qubits Actually Mean?

This is where most coverage gets things wrong. A qubit is not just a faster bit. It can exist in a superposition of 0 and 1 simultaneously, which allows quantum computers to explore many solutions at once rather than one at a time. In theory, that makes certain problems, like factoring large numbers or optimizing complex logistics, dramatically faster to solve.

In practice, qubits are fragile. A tiny temperature shift, a stray vibration, or electromagnetic noise causes decoherence, wich is when the qubit loses its quantum properties and the calculation fails. Managing this is the core engineering challenge in the entire field.

At 25 qubits, you can run meaningful quantum experiments, test gate designs, and experiment with error-correction protocols. But for true quantum advantage, meaning doing something usefully faster than any classical computer, most experts estimate you need hundreds or thousands of error-corrected qubits. IBM's Heron processor runs at 156 qubits. Google's Willow chip demonstrated computations that would take classical supercomputers an astronomical amount of time. The scale gap is real.

So 25 qubits is not symbolic. It's also nowhere near useful for the applications that make quantum computing exciting.

The gap is large. That's not a dismissal of India's efforts, just context. The US and China have been investing in quantum since the early 2010s. India is catching up from a later start, which makes the talent pipeline more important than the qubit count right now.

Is India's National Quantum Mission on Track?

India approved the National Quantum Mission in April 2023 with a budget of Rs 6,003 crore over eight years. The targets are 50-qubit systems by 2027, and 1,000-qubit indigenous systems by 2028 to 2031. MIT Bengaluru's hub is one of the early nodes in this broader effort, not the whole program.

The talent problem is where India faces its steepest climb. India has roughly 300 to 400 researchers actively working in quantum science. The US has several thousand, and China has been estimated at over 10,000. Hardware is hard to build, but you can source components internationally. You can't import ten years of expertise in a semester.

That's what makes the 100-engineers-by-December target relevant. It's a small number in global terms. The seperate question is whether India's research ecosystem will retain those engineers, or whether they'll leave for better-funded labs abroad. Brain drain has been a quiet problem in every earlier deep-tech push.

Should Indian Tech Professionals Care About This Now?

Honestly, if you're a software engineer or startup founder today, quantum computing is not something you should be building for. The applications that work in production, like molecule simulation for pharma and certain optimization problems, require fault-tolerant quantum computers that don't exist yet for anyone.

But if you're a student in computer science, physics, or electrical engineering, the window to develop quantum skills is open. IBM and Google already offer cloud-accessible quantum hardware. Qiskit, IBM's open-source framework, and Cirq, Google's equivalent, let you run real quantum programs today on machines more capable than MIT Bengaluru's current hub.

Awareness now costs nothing. Expertise compounds over time. And if the push succeds as planned, those domestic 1,000-qubit systems will need engineers who've been working in the field for years, not months.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Quantum-Hub@MAHE?

It's a quantum computing research and training facility at Manipal Institute of Technology in Bengaluru, opened October 2026 with a 25-qubit system. Its primary mission is engineering education, hardware experimentation, and start-up incubation, not commercial quantum services. Partners include QuantrolOx, Bluefors, and Qblox.

Is 25 qubits enough to be useful for real problems?

For teaching and experimental work, yes. For commercially relevant tasks, no. Most estimates suggest you need thousands to millions of error-corrected qubits for practical quantum advantage on problems like drug discovery or logistics optimization. At 25 qubits you can test circuits, but nothing a classical computer can't already handle faster.

How does India compare to the US and China in quantum computing?

The US leads with IBM and Google operating systems above 1,000 qubits and years of private investment. China's Zuchongzhi processor runs at 504 qubits, backed by heavy state funding. India is at 25 qubits in its first dedicated hub, with national targets aiming for 1,000-qubit indigenous systems by the late 2020s.

What is India's National Quantum Mission?

A government program approved in April 2023 with a Rs 6,003 crore budget over eight years. Targets include 50-qubit systems by 2027 and 1,000-qubit systems by 2028 to 2031. MIT Bengaluru's hub is one of the early nodes in this mission, focused on building talent and hardware research capacity.

When will quantum computing actually be useful for Indian businesses?

Practical quantum advantage for most industries, including finance, pharma, and logistics, is likely 10 or more years away for any country. Near-term value is in talent development and hardware know-how. Indian businesses should monitor the space but don't need to build for quantum applications yet.

The Short Version

India's new 25-qubit quantum hub is a real step, not a landmark one. It won't crack encryption or accelerate drug discovery. What it will do is seed a small but important talent pipeline at a moment when the global quantum race is early enough that catching up is still possible. The National Quantum Mission's targets are ambitious and the 2028 to 2031 timeline is achievable if funding holds. For now, think of MIT Bengaluru's facility as India's first quantum training ground, where the engineers who will matter in 2035 are starting to learn.
